newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-NEVADA COMMISSION TO DEBATE TYSON'S FATE.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-NEVADA COMMISSION TO DEBATE TYSON'S FATE.

text.p: The Nevada State Athletic Commission was set to begin debating the fate of Mike Tyson on Tuesday, and one member said the fighter would probably be banned from boxing for biting Evander Holyfield's ears in their world heavyweight title bout.

Luther Mack, one of five members of the commission that will discipline Tyson, told ABC's "Good Morning America": "We can suspend him because what he did was not tolerated ... certainly we would do something in that area -- exactly in terms of months, years at this point in time, I do not know."

Holyfield's attorney, speaking on the same television programme Tuesday, said his client, the World Boxing Association champion, accepted an apology made by Tyson Monday but wanted the commission to preserve the integrity of boxing.
The commission was due to meet later on Tuesday to decide what action should be taken against Tyson after he bit both of the champion's ears in Saturday's heavyweight title fight in Las Vegas.

The fight was stopped after the third round and Tyson was disqualified after he ignored a warning from referee Mills Lane for biting a chunk from the top of Holyfield's right ear and proceeded to chew on the champion's left ear.
Holyfield will require reconstructive plastic surgery and his lawyer Jim Thomas has not ruled out taking legal action against Tyson for the injury.
Among its options, the commission, which regulates boxing in Nevada, could fine, suspend or ban Tyson from the sport. It could also revoke his boxing license.

On Monday, the commission's chairman Elias Ghanem told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that he favoured taking all of Tyson's $30 million purse for the fight. But under state laws the commission can only take 10 percent of his earnings from the bout.
Tyson, the self-proclaimed "baddest man on the planet", appeared contrite at a news conference Monday and apologised for his actions.

He apologised for "snapping" in the ring and begged for forgiveness, saying he would accept the commission's punishment. In what many boxing insiders believed was a veiled appeal for clemency, Tyson asked only that he not be hit with a lifetime ban from boxing.
Tyson made a point of including an apology to the state commission "that has always treated me fairly."
Holyfield's attorney said the champion wanted the commission to take "meaningful" sanctions that would preserve the sport's integrity.
"He (Holyfield) certainly accepts the apology and hopes that it's sincere," Thomas said in the television interview.

"He doesn't have any personal desire to hurt or punish Mike Tyson ... Evander wants something done that will help preserve the integrity of that sport, and for that to happen some very meaningful sanctions need to be issued by the commission."
